title: Constant-competitive online matching on the line
formal: Does there exist a deterministic online algorithm and a universal \(C\ge 1\) such that, for every \(k\ge 1\), every known set of k server positions on the real line and every sequence of k arriving client positions, it irrevocably matches each arriving client to one unused server with total distance at most C times the cost of an optimal offline matching?

source_formulation.text: It is still an open question whether constant-competitive algorithms exist for OMM-Line.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

context:
Decisions made before the future is known. Regret and competitive ratios compare performance to a specified benchmark.

Source of the specific model: Permutation Strikes Back: The Power of Recourse in Online Metric Matching (APPROX/RANDOM, 2020). Question location: Explicit open question on PDF page 2.

Both introductory passages concern irrevocable bipartite matching of arriving clients to a known set of servers on the line, with sum of distances as cost and worst-case arrival order. Their deterministic \(O(\log  k)\) benchmark and deterministic constant-lower-bound discussion support the deterministic constant-competitive question. Randomized algorithms against oblivious adversaries form a distinct variant; the general-metric randomized discussion and recourse results are not substituted for a deterministic no-recourse guarantee.

sentences: Online metric matching assigns each arriving client to an unused server and pays the distance between them.
On the real line, the source asks whether a constant competitive ratio is possible when assignments are irrevocable.
Logarithmic lower bounds for several natural algorithm families do not rule out every possible strategy.
The surrounding paper permits reassignment to study how much limited recourse can help.
The original question isolates whether one-dimensional order alone can overcome uncertainty about future clients, without any later opportunity to repair the matching.

definitions: Servers are individually labeled and their positions are known before requests arrive. Client positions are revealed one at a time; the algorithm must match each to one unused server before seeing the next. Positions may coincide. An assignment cannot later be changed. Cost is the sum of absolute differences of matched positions. The offline optimum sees the complete client sequence and uses each server once. The inequality is required even when that optimum is zero. C is independent of k, coordinates and arrival order; there is no additive term. The model measures matching cost with no restriction on internal computation. The algorithm is deterministic, so worst-case fixed sequences and adaptively chosen sequences yield the same universal guarantee. No randomness, random-order promise or recourse is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of the deterministic universal constant-competitive strategy, or prove its logical negation with the same unrestricted line inputs and irrevocable matching convention. A randomized guarantee, a restricted-arrival guarantee or an algorithm allowing reassignment does not settle this formulation.

changes: Aligned the deterministic, arbitrary-arrival, no-recourse convention across the two consolidated source occurrences.
